title: Exit Replay and Counterfactual Workbook
body:
Purpose:
A compact, action-oriented workbook for running an ‘exit replay’ — a focused postmortem whose primary goal is to 1) reconstruct the sequence of events that led to a lost renewal, 2) surface the smallest set of high-confidence root causes, and 3) produce counterfactual experiments that would have materially changed outcome probability. Use this during the 60–90 minute loss review and preserve artifacts for QBRs and product backlogs.

How to use this doc (quick flow):
- Pre-read (10–15 min): owner collects timeline notes, last three contract touchpoints, support tickets, and executive emails.
- Loss review session (60–90 min): facilitator walks team through sections below; capture evidence and votes live.
- Post-session (1–2 weeks): owners deliver highest-confidence counterfactual experiments as tickets and assign owners for quick wins.

Section A — One-line loss thesis:
- Example prompt: Why did the account choose to leave, in one sentence? Identify the dominant, attributable reason.
- One-line thesis (fill in): 

Section B — Executive summary (template):
- Contract size — last ARR committed: $
- Renewal date: 
- Reason communicated by customer (short quote): 
- Net churn driver (pick up to 2): product fit | cost economics | org change | procurement | performance/reliability | security/compliance | support experience | competitive displacement | other
- Recommended immediate intervention: (quick win / stop-gap)

Section C — Chronology map (timeboxed):
- Use discrete time windows (Pre-sale baseline, 0-90 days post-deploy, last 180 days pre-renewal, final 30 days). For each window, capture: expected outcomes, what actually happened, signals observed, owner(s).
- Sample entries (replace with account specifics):
  * Pre-sale baseline (sales pitch): committed throughput target: 5 TPS, promised <200ms p99 on hosted API.
  * 0-90d: integration lag (SDK mismatch), two SRE tickets raised (SUP-112, SUP-145), no formal onboarding workshop scheduled.
  * Last 180d: token costs above forecast, engineering requested model quantization guidance (PRD-448), product roadmap item deferred.
  * Final 30d: procurement cited price spike and lack of cost-forecasting; renewal call ended with customer stating they had alternative provider proof-of-concept.

Section D — Decision forkpoints (where a different choice could have changed trajectory):
- Forkpoint 1 (date): e.g., skip onboarding workshop -> consequence: integration drift, escalating support load. Counterfactual experiment: mandate onboarding within contract; deliver onboarding playbook + 1 dedicated SE day.
- Forkpoint 2 (date): e.g., failure to provide cost forecast for high-volume queries -> consequence: surprise billing. Counterfactual: auto-generate per-route cost estimator, share monthly burn ahead-of-renewal.

Section E — Evidence log (concise):
- Primary evidence types: support tickets, slack threads, billing exports, SLA/latency traces, sales notes, contract addendum, executive emails.
- Example formatted lines (paste actual artifacts):
  * SUP-112: elevated p99 latency on 2024-10-16 (trace id 0x9f1c).
  * Billing export (Q3-2024): overage charges $12k above forecast.
  * Slack: sales->cs thread 2024-11-02 "cancel if no cost forecast".

Section F — Root cause analysis (scoring rubric):
- For each candidate root cause, assign 3 scores (1-5 integers): Impact (how much it moved the needle), Likelihood (evidence strength), Preventability (team could have prevented). Sum=priority score.
- Example table (enter as lines):
  * Cause: lack of cost visibility | Impact: 5 | Likelihood: 4 | Preventability: 5 | Sum:14 | Evidence refs: Billing export, Slack thread
  * Cause: onboarding gap | Impact: 3 | Likelihood: 3 | Preventability: 4 | Sum:10 | Evidence refs: SUP-112, onboarding notes

Section G — Counterfactual experiments (actionable and testable):
- Each experiment should specify: hypothesis, minimal intervention, acceptance criteria (KPI delta), owner, timeframe, required resources.
- Example entries (copy into tickets):
  1) Hypothesis: If we provided a per-route cost estimator during trial, renewals where forecasted spend <5% variance will increase by X.
     - Minimal intervention: engineer builds a simple per-route cost calculator + CS playbook.
     - Acceptance criteria: 80% of pilot accounts report within 10% of actual spend in first 30 days.
     - Owner: Product ops / CS SE.
     - Timeframe: 6 weeks.
  2) Hypothesis: Mandatory onboarding within first 30 days reduces critical tickets by 50% by day 90.
     - Minimal intervention: scheduling workflow + one SE day included in contract.
     - Acceptance criteria: 50% reduction in P1/P2 tickets.

Section H — Quick wins (to ship in 30 days):
- Quick wins should be low-effort, high-visibility. Assign owner and due date.
- Example quick wins lines:
  * Add "expected monthly spend" field to contract template + CS automation to compute estimates | Owner: Jamal Rivera | Due: 2025-03-20
  * Create a one-page onboarding checklist and schedule automation | Owner: Priya Desai | Due: 2025-03-10

Section I — Longer-term changes (product/process):
- Product candidates: cost-forecasting tooling, route-level metering UI, automated onboarding wizard, SLA-based routing fallback.
- Process candidates: renewal smoke tests, contract-level cost protection clause, quarterly CFO sync for large spenders.

Section J — Success metrics and guardrails for future renewals:
- KPIs to track for similar accounts: 30/60/90 day ticket volume, variance between forecast and actual spend, time-to-first-value (days), p99 latency breaches per month, renewal NPS.
- Suggested guardrail thresholds: forecast variance > 15% => escalation; p99 latency breaches > 2/month => remediation window.

Section K — Communication plan (to execs & product):
- Short note to execs (template): subject line: Account X renewal loss: short thesis + two mitigations + ask (budget/eng resource).
- Follow-up to product: link to counterfactual experiments and ask for prioritization scoring during next roadmap review.

Section L — Retrospective notes (open items and unresolved questions):
- Example prompts: What evidence do we still lack? Which stakeholders were not engaged early enough? Which assumptions are weakest?
- Open items (fill in):
  * Missing cost-model audit from finance for Q3-2024.
  * Confirm whether competitive POC showed meaningful cost delta or just promotional credits.

Section M — Postmortem sign-offs and distribution:
- Sign-off roles: CS lead, Solutions Eng lead, Product ops, and Finance rep (for billing related losses).
- Distribution list: AM, CS leadership, Product, SRE, Finance, Legal (if contract concerns).

Appendix A — Facilitator checklist (for the 60–90 minute session):
- Gather artifacts 48h in advance.
- Pre-annotate timeline.
- Bring VLAN/exported traces, billing CSV, and renewal call recording.
- Timebox sections: 10min thesis + 20min timeline + 20min root cause voting + 20min counterfactuals + 10min next steps.

Appendix B — Example completed mini-workbook (fictionalized):
- One-line thesis: account left because unexpected token costs caused a procurement freeze in Q4.
- Top root cause (scored): lack of cost visibility | Impact 5 | Likelihood 4 | Preventability 5 | Sum 14.
- Top counterfactual: auto-send monthly burn forecast + include cost protection clause for first quarter.
- Quick wins: add spend field to contract (owner: Jamal).

Notes and version history:
- 2025-02-11: initial draft by Leah Kim (CS).
- 2025-02-25: added scoring rubric and facilitator checklist (Jamal Rivera).
- 2025-03-04: clarified evidence log format and appended example workbook (Priya Desai).

Document footer: This workbook is intended for internal use. Keep copies attached to the account record and link to the QBR artifacts for continuous learning and product prioritization.
